summary.text: After extracting the multiples of $p$ from each factorial, the proof shows that every full block of $p$-coprime factors is unchanged modulo $p^{3r}$ by expanding its shifted product through degree two; the linear and quadratic terms vanish by generalized Wolstenholme congruences for the reciprocal and reciprocal-square sums. For odd indices, the half-factorials are handled by reflection and doubling of half-blocks, whose resulting factor $4^{p^r-p^{r-1}}$ telescopes and cancels the corresponding power of $4$; for even indices, the balanced full-block powers cancel directly.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(m)=\frac{\Gamma(9m+1)\Gamma(2m+1)\Gamma(\tfrac32m+1)}
 {\Gamma(\tfrac92m+1)\Gamma(4m+1)\Gamma(3m+1)\Gamma(m+1)}.
\]
Thus this is the factorial ratio in the question, with a factorial at a nonintegral argument interpreted by the gamma function. Since the assertion that all these numbers are integers is itself only conjectural, the precise statement proved here is the following conditional one: assume that every \(a(m)\) is an integer. Then, for every prime \(p\geq5\) and positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
We prove this statement. Throughout, congruences and calculations involving inverses are performed in the indicated residue ring. Every integer prime to \(p\) is a unit in every ring \(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z\).

## 1. Harmonic congruences

We begin with two harmonic-sum facts that will control products in blocks of length \(p^r\).

For any \(N=p^s\), let \(U_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^\times\). Since \(p\geq5\), both 2 and 3 are units modulo \(N\). Put
\[
 S_2=\sum_{u\in U_N}u^2.
\]
Multiplication by 2 permutes \(U_N\), and therefore
\[
 S_2=\sum_{u\in U_N}(2u)^2=4S_2.
\]
Thus \(3S_2=0\), and 3 is invertible, so \(S_2=0\). Inversion also permutes the unit group, hence
\[
 \sum_{u\in U_N}u^{-2}=\sum_{u\in U_N}u^2=0. \tag{1}
\]

The integers \(0\leq k<p^r\) with \(p\nmid k\) form a complete set of representatives for the units modulo \(p^r\). Moreover, each interval of length \(p^r\) beginning at a multiple of \(p^r\) gives the same representatives. Consequently, for every nonnegative integer \(b\),
\[
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq k<bp^r\\p\nmid k}} k^{-2}=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^r\mathbb Z. \tag{2}
\]

We also need the stronger inverse-sum congruence
\[
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq k<bp^r\\p\nmid k}}k^{-1}=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^{2r}\mathbb Z. \tag{3}
\]
Here is a proof. Set \(M=bp^r\) and let \(F\) be the set of integers \(k\) with \(0\leq k<M\) and \(p\nmid k\). The map \(k\mapsto M-k\) permutes \(F\): zero is not in \(F\), and because \(p\mid M\), one has \(p\nmid(M-k)\) whenever \(p\nmid k\). In \(\mathbb Z/p^{2r}\mathbb Z\), write
\[
 S=\sum_{k\in F}k^{-1},\qquad
 T=\sum_{k\in F}k^{-1}(M-k)^{-1}.
\]
Pairing the summands under \(k\mapsto M-k\) gives
\[
 2S=\sum_{k\in F}\bigl(k^{-1}+(M-k)^{-1}\bigr)=MT. \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the expression in parentheses is \(M/[k(M-k)]\).

Reduce \(bT\) modulo \(p^r\). Since \(M=bp^r\), we have \(M-k\equiv-k\pmod {p^r}\), so
\[
 bT\equiv-b\sum_{k\in F}k^{-2}\equiv0\pmod {p^r}
\]
by (2). Thus \(bT\) is divisible by \(p^r\), and hence
\[
 MT=p^r(bT)\equiv0\pmod {p^{2r}}.
\]
Equation (4), together with the invertibility of 2, proves (3).

We will repeatedly use the elementary lifting observation that if an element \(z\) modulo \(p^t\) reduces to zero modulo \(p^a\), where \(a\leq t\), then
\[
 p^{t-a}z=0\quad\text{modulo }p^t. \tag{5}
\]
This simply says that a representative of \(z\) is divisible by \(p^a\).

## 2. Invariance of a full prime-to-\(p\) block

Fix \(p,r\), and work in
\[
 R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r}\mathbb Z.
\]
Define
\[
 G=\prod_{\substack{0\leq \ell<p^r\\p\nmid\ell}}\ell\in R.
\]
We claim that every shifted block has the same product:
\[
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq \ell<p^r\\p\nmid\ell}}(ip^r+\ell)=G
 \qquad(i\geq0). \tag{6}
\]
For a permissible \(\ell\), factor
\[
 ip^r+\ell=\ell\left(1+ip^r\ell^{-1}\right).
\]
Put \(x_\ell=ip^r\ell^{-1}\). Any product of three \(x_\ell\)'s is zero in \(R\), because it contains \(p^{3r}\). When all triple products of a finite family \(x_j\) vanish, direct expansion gives
\[
 2\prod_j(1+x_j)
 =2+2\sum_jx_j+\left(\sum_jx_j\right)^2-\sum_jx_j^2. \tag{7}
\]
This is simply the product expansion through degree two: the right side equals
\(2+2\sum x_j+2\sum_{j<k}x_jx_k\).

Now (3), for one block, says that \(\sum\ell^{-1}\) is zero modulo \(p^{2r}\). By (5),
\[
 p^r\sum\ell^{-1}=0\quad\text{in }R.
\]
Similarly, (2) and (5) give
\[
 p^{2r}\sum\ell^{-2}=0\quad\text{in }R.
\]
It follows that \(\sum x_\ell=0\) and \(\sum x_\ell^2=0\). Formula (7) therefore gives
\(2\prod(1+x_\ell)=2\). Since 2 is a unit, \(\prod(1+x_\ell)=1\), proving (6).

Dividing \([0,bp^r)\) into \(b\) blocks of length \(p^r\), we obtain the fundamental product congruence
\[
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq k<bp^r\\p\nmid k}}k=G^b
 \quad\text{in }R. \tag{8}
\]
Every product in (8) is a unit in \(R\).

## 3. Stripping multiples of \(p\) from factorials

For every nonnegative integer \(N\), separating the factors of \(N!\) according as they are or are not divisible by \(p\) gives
\[
 N!=\left(\prod_{\substack{1\leq k\leq N\\p\nmid k}}k\right)
 p^{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}\lfloor N/p\rfloor!. \tag{9}
\]
If \(N=bp^r\), the endpoint \(N\) is divisible by \(p\), so the prime-to-\(p\) product may equivalently be taken over \(0\leq k<bp^r\). Also \(N/p=bp^{r-1}\). Thus
\[
 (bp^r)!=Q_b\,p^{bp^{r-1}}(bp^{r-1})!, \qquad
 Q_b:=\prod_{\substack{0\leq k<bp^r\\p\nmid k}}k. \tag{10}
\]
Modulo \(p^{3r}\), equation (8) says \(Q_b=G^b\).

## 4. The even case

Suppose first that \(n=2\mu\). Directly evaluating all gamma factors at integers gives
\[
 a(2M)\,(9M)!(8M)!(6M)!(2M)!
 =(18M)!(4M)!(3M)!. \tag{11}
\]
Let
\[
 x=a(2\mu p^r),\qquad y=a(2\mu p^{r-1}),
\]
which are integers by the integrality hypothesis. Apply (10) to every factorial in (11), first with \(M=\mu p^r\) and then with \(M=\mu p^{r-1}\). The total extracted power of \(p\) on the right at level \(r\) is
\[
 (18+4+3)\mu p^{r-1}=25\mu p^{r-1},
\]
and on the left it is
\[
 (9+8+6+2)\mu p^{r-1}=25\mu p^{r-1}.
\]
The lower-level factorial products are exactly those appearing in the identity for \(y\). Since all factorials and powers of \(p\) involved are nonzero integers, ordinary cancellation in \(\mathbb Z\) yields
\[
 x\,Q_{9\mu}Q_{8\mu}Q_{6\mu}Q_{2\mu}
 =Q_{18\mu}Q_{4\mu}Q_{3\mu}\,y. \tag{12}
\]
Modulo \(p^{3r}\), (8) turns the two prime-to-\(p\) products into
\[
 G^{(9+8+6+2)\mu}=G^{25\mu}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 G^{(18+4+3)\mu}=G^{25\mu}.
\]
This common factor is a unit, so it can be canceled from (12). Hence \(x\equiv y\pmod {p^{3r}}\). This proves the result when \(n\) is even.

## 5. Half-block identities

The odd case involves half-integer gamma values and therefore requires a refinement of (8). Continue to work in \(R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r}\mathbb Z\). Put
\[
 U=\{k:0\leq k<p^r,\ p\nmid k\},
 \qquad
 L=\{\ell\in U:2\ell\leq p^r\}.
\]
Since \(p^r\) is odd, the involution \(k\mapsto p^r-k\) partitions \(U\) into pairs with exactly one member in \(L\). Therefore
\[
 |U|=p^r-p^{r-1},\qquad
 2|L|=p^r-p^{r-1}. \tag{13}
\]
We have the two product decompositions
\[
 \prod_{k\in U}f(k)
 =\prod_{\ell\in L}f(\ell)f(p^r-\ell), \tag{14}
\]
\[
 \prod_{k\in U}f(k)
 =\prod_{\ell\in L}f(2\ell)f(p^r-2\ell). \tag{15}
\]
For (15), the even elements of \(U\) are \(2\ell\) with \(\ell\in L\), while every odd element is uniquely \(p^r-2\ell\). The fact that \(p\geq5\) ensures that multiplication by 2 does not introduce divisibility by \(p\).

The inverse-square sum on the half-set satisfies
\[
 \sum_{\ell\in L}\ell^{-2}=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^r\mathbb Z. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, (14) has an additive analogue. Under reflection, \(p^r-\ell\equiv-\ell\pmod {p^r}\), so inverse squares agree. Thus the full sum over \(U\), which is zero by (1), is twice the sum over \(L\). Canceling 2 proves (16). Consequently, by (5),
\[
 p^{2r}\sum_{\ell\in L}\ell^{-2}=0\quad\text{in }R. \tag{17}
\]

Write \(c=p^r\in R\), and define
\[
 A=\prod_{\ell\in L}\ell,
\quad
 R_1=\prod_{\ell\in L}(1-c\ell^{-1}),
\quad
 R_h=\prod_{\ell\in L}(1-c(2\ell)^{-1}).
\]
We claim
\[
 R_h^2=R_1. \tag{18}
\]
To see this, put \(x_\ell=-c\ell^{-1}\) and
\(y_\ell=2^{-1}x_\ell=-c(2\ell)^{-1}\). Triple products among either the \(x_\ell\)'s or the \(y_\ell\)'s vanish because \(c^3=p^{3r}=0\) in \(R\). Also, by (17),
\[
 \sum x_\ell^2=\sum y_\ell^2=0.
\]
Let \(S_x=\sum x_\ell\), \(S_y=\sum y_\ell\). Then \(S_x=2S_y\), and \(S_y^3=0\). Formula (7) gives
\[
 2R_1=2+2S_x+S_x^2,
\qquad
 2R_h=2+2S_y+S_y^2.
\]
Substituting \(S_x=2S_y\) and expanding, the difference between
\((2R_h)^2\) and \(4R_1\) is a multiple of \(S_y^3\), hence is zero. Canceling the unit 4 proves (18).

Now let
\[
 G=\prod_{k\in U}k,
\quad h=|L|,
\quad P_2=\prod_{\ell\in L}2\ell=2^hA.
\]
From (14) and (15),
\[
 G=A\prod_{\ell\in L}(p^r-\ell)
   =P_2\prod_{\ell\in L}(p^r-2\ell). \tag{19}
\]
For each \(\ell\in L\), elementary factorization gives
\[
 \ell(1-c\ell^{-1})=-(p^r-\ell),
\]
and likewise
\[
 2\ell(1-c(2\ell)^{-1})=-(p^r-2\ell).
\]
Therefore
\[
 AR_1=(-1)^h\prod_{\ell\in L}(p^r-\ell),
\qquad
 P_2R_h=(-1)^h\prod_{\ell\in L}(p^r-2\ell). \tag{20}
\]
Combining (19) and (20),
\[
 A^2R_1=(-1)^hG,
\qquad
 P_2^2R_h=(-1)^hG. \tag{21}
\]
The quantities \(A,R_1,R_h\) are units: \(A\) is visibly a product of units, and every factor \(1-z\) in \(R_1\) has inverse \(1+z+z^2\), since \(z^3=0\); then (18) implies that \(R_h\) is a unit as well.

Using \(P_2=2^hA\), equations (21) imply, after canceling \(A^2\),
\[
 R_1=2^{2h}R_h.
\]
Together with \(R_1=R_h^2\), and canceling \(R_h\), this gives
\[
 R_h=2^{2h},\qquad R_1=2^{4h}.
\]
Substituting into (21), and using (13), yields the useful explicit formula
\[
 G=(-1)^h4^{\,p^r-p^{r-1}}A^2. \tag{22}
\]

We next prove the half-block shift relation. For \(q\geq0\), define
\[
 B_q=\prod_{\ell\in L}(qp^r+\ell).
\]
Then
\[
 B_q=4^{\,p^r-p^{r-1}}B_{q+1}. \tag{23}
\]
Let
\[
 A_q=\prod_{\ell\in L}((q+1)p^r-\ell).
\]
Reflection decomposition (14), applied to the shifted full block, together with the full-block invariance (6), gives
\[
 B_qA_q=G. \tag{24}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 ((q+1)p^r+\ell)((q+1)p^r-\ell)
 =-\ell^2\left(1-w_\ell\right),

after setting
\[
 w_\ell=-\,(q+1)^2p^{2r}\ell^{-2}.
\]
Products \(w_iw_j\) vanish modulo \(p^{3r}\), since they contain \(p^{4r}\), and their sum vanishes by (17). Hence
\[
 \prod_{\ell\in L}(1+w_\ell)=1+\sum_{\ell\in L}w_\ell=1.
\]
It follows that
\[
 B_{q+1}A_q=(-1)^hA^2. \tag{25}
\]
Equations (22), (24), and (25) give
\[
 B_qA_q=4^{\,p^r-p^{r-1}}B_{q+1}A_q.
\]
Every factor in \(A_q\) is prime to \(p\), so \(A_q\) is a unit and can be canceled. This proves (23). Iterating it gives
\[
 B_a=4^{\,k(p^r-p^{r-1})}B_{a+k} \qquad(a,k\geq0). \tag{26}
\]

Finally, if a prime-to-\(p\) product stops halfway through a block, full-block decomposition and the definition of \(L\) give
\[
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq j<q p^r+(p^r-1)/2+1\\p\nmid j}}j
 =G^qB_q. \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, the first \(q\) full blocks contribute \(G^q\) by (6), and because \(p^r\) is odd, the remaining allowed offsets \(0\leq\ell\leq(p^r-1)/2\) are exactly the elements of \(L\).

## 6. Gamma evaluation in the odd case

For every nonnegative integer \(k\), the recurrence \(\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)\), starting from \(\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi\), gives
\[
 \Gamma\left(k+\tfrac12\right)
 =\frac{(2k)!}{4^k k!}\sqrt\pi. \tag{28}
\]
Using (28) in the definition of \(a(2\mu+1)\), canceling the two occurrences of \(\sqrt\pi\), and applying the ordinary factorial recurrence to the adjacent factorials gives
\[
 a(2\mu+1)(8\mu+4)!(2\mu+1)!(3\mu+1)!
 =4^{6\mu+3}(4\mu+2)!(9\mu+4)!. \tag{29}
\]
Equivalently, for every odd positive integer \(m\),
\[
 a(m)(4m)!m!\left(\frac{3m-1}{2}\right)!
 =4^{3m}(2m)!\left(\frac{9m-1}{2}\right)!. \tag{30}
\]

We also record the factorial-stripping formula for these half-sized arguments. If \(a\) is odd, then
\[
 \frac{ap^r-1}{2}
 =\frac{a-1}{2}p^r+\frac{p^r-1}{2}. \tag{31}
\]
This follows by writing both \(a\) and \(p^r\) as odd numbers. Applying (9), and observing that
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{q p^r+(p^r-1)/2}{p}\right\rfloor
 =q p^{r-1}+\frac{p^{r-1}-1}{2}, \tag{32}
\]
we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left(\frac{ap^r-1}{2}\right)!
 ={}&H_{(a-1)/2}\,
 p^{\,((a-1)/2)p^{r-1}+(p^{r-1}-1)/2}
 \left(\frac{ap^{r-1}-1}{2}\right)!, \
 H_q:={}&\prod_{\substack{0\leq j<q p^r+(p^r-1)/2+1\\p\nmid j}}j.
 \end{aligned} \tag{33}
\]
Formula (27) says, modulo \(p^{3r}\),
\[
 H_q=G^qB_q. \tag{34}
\]

## 7. The odd case

Now suppose that \(n\) is odd. Let
\[
 x=a(np^r),\qquad y=a(np^{r-1}),
\]
again integers by hypothesis. Apply (30) to \(m=np^r\) and \(m=np^{r-1}\). Strip one level of multiples of \(p\) from the three ordinary factorials using (10), and from the two half-sized factorials using (33).

On the left side of (30), the extracted exponent of \(p\) is
\[
 E=\left(5n+\frac{3n-1}{2}\right)p^{r-1}
   +\frac{p^{r-1}-1}{2}.
\]
On the right it is the same, because
\[
 2n+\frac{9n-1}{2}=5n+\frac{3n-1}{2}. \tag{35}
\]
Also split
\[
 4^{3np^r}=4^{3np^{r-1}}\,4^{3n(p^r-p^{r-1})}.
\]
The lower-level factorial identity is precisely the one containing \(y\). Canceling the common nonzero integer consisting of the extracted power \(p^E\) and the lower-level left factorial product gives
\[
 x\,Q_{4n}Q_nH_{(3n-1)/2}
 =4^{3n(p^r-p^{r-1})}Q_{2n}H_{(9n-1)/2}\,y. \tag{36}
\]

Reduce (36) modulo \(p^{3r}\). By (8) and (34), its prime-to-\(p\) factors become
\[
 Q_{4n}=G^{4n},\quad Q_n=G^n,\quad Q_{2n}=G^{2n},
\]
\[
 H_{(3n-1)/2}=G^{(3n-1)/2}B_{(3n-1)/2},
\]
\[
 H_{(9n-1)/2}=G^{(9n-1)/2}B_{(9n-1)/2}.
\]
The powers of \(G\) on the two sides agree, because
\[
 4n+n+\frac{3n-1}{2}
 =2n+\frac{9n-1}{2}.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 \frac{9n-1}{2}=\frac{3n-1}{2}+3n.
\]
Thus the telescoping identity (26), with
\(a=(3n-1)/2\) and \(k=3n\), gives
\[
 B_{(3n-1)/2}
 =4^{3n(p^r-p^{r-1})}B_{(9n-1)/2}. \tag{37}
\]
After using (37), equation (36) has exactly the same multiplier on \(x\) and on \(y\). This multiplier is a product of powers of \(G\), of 4, and of prime-to-\(p\) factors, so it is a unit modulo \(p^{3r}\). Canceling it yields
\[
 x\equiv y\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
This proves the odd case.

Every positive integer \(n\) is either even or odd, so the two cases together establish, for all primes \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
 \boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}}.
\]
As stated at the outset, the congruence applies to the integer values represented by the factorial ratio; the integrality of the entire sequence is the separate premise needed to make this an integer congruence for every index.
